name: Bromantane
lead: Bromantane (also spelled bromantan; Russian brand name Ladasten) is a synthetic adamantane derivative, chemically N-(4-bromophenyl)adamantan-2-amine, that is related to amantadine and memantine. It is described in the literature as an atypical stimulant and anxiolytic and as an "actoprotector", a term used in Russian pharmacology for synthetic adaptogens said to raise resistance to physical and psychological stress. [1][2][3]

Bromantane was developed in the Soviet Union at the Zakusov Institute of Pharmacology in Moscow and is a prescription drug in Russia for neurasthenia (asthenia). It is not approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, and it has been on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list since 1997. [2] In looksmaxxing and nootropic circles it is discussed as a supplement for motivation, mood, stress resilience and recovery rather than as a direct appearance treatment. [7][8]

Most published human data are from Russian-language journals. Animal studies report that it increases the activity of enzymes involved in dopamine synthesis. [2][4][5] Proponents' claims about testosterone, prolactin and sexual function that circulate in forums have not been tested in published human trials.

paras: In Russia bromantane is approved for neurasthenia, a fatigue-and-weakness syndrome, and it is described as combining mild stimulant and anxiolytic effects. [2] Russian military and sports medicine reportedly used it to shorten recovery after heavy physical exertion. [2]

Outside Russia it is sold or traded as a nootropic or research chemical. Forum users describe taking it for motivation, drive, calmer mood and as a complement to training and stress management. [7][8]

Unlike amphetamine-type stimulants, bromantane is reported to act mainly by raising the expression of tyrosine hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, enzymes in dopamine synthesis, rather than primarily blocking the dopamine transporter. [2] A 1995 rat study reported changes in dopamine, serotonin and their metabolites in several brain regions after acute and chronic administration, and a microdialysis study in the same year examined dopamine release in the striatum. [4][5]

Researchers also describe effects on protein kinase signalling and neurotrophin expression in animals, but the receptor responsible has not been identified and the full mechanism remains unclear. [2] Reviews of Russian adaptogen research list bromantane among synthetic actoprotectors. [3][9]

Reported oral bioavailability is about 42%, with onset in roughly 1.5 to 2 hours, a duration of 8 to 12 hours and an elimination half-life near 11 hours in humans. The main metabolite is 6-beta-hydroxybromantane. [2]

The best-cited human evidence is a multicentre Russian study of 728 patients with asthenia that reported symptom improvement on clinical global scales, with persistence after treatment ended. [2] A 2009 placebo comparison in neurasthenia is also cited. [2] Most of this literature is in Russian-language journals, and independent replication in Western trials has not been published. [2][6]
No controlled study has examined bromantane for appearance outcomes, body composition, hormone levels in healthy people, or the stress-and-recovery effects claimed in forums.

Russian sources describe the drug as well tolerated. In the multicentre study, side effects were reported in about 3% of patients, none serious, and 0.8% stopped treatment because of them. [2] Absence of dependence and withdrawal is reported mainly in Russian-language and animal work. [2][6]

Animal toxicity studies at very high doses have reported neurological effects, which some authors attribute to anticholinergic activity. [2] Long-term safety in healthy adults using it recreationally has not been studied in published trials.

Amantadine was developed as an influenza antiviral in the 1960s, and its dopaminergic effects were noticed in 1969. Bromantane emerged in the 1980s from Soviet work on adamantane derivatives intended to increase resistance to extreme conditions; a Russian review describes 329 novel adamantane derivatives synthesised and studied, of which bromantane was among the most promising. [2][6]

At the 1996 Atlanta Olympics several Russian athletes tested positive, bringing the drug to international attention, and WADA listed it as a stimulant and masking agent in 1997. [2][1] It was repurposed in Russia as a neurasthenia treatment, with the Ladasten brand approved in the late 2000s. [2]
Bromantane is prescription-only in Russia, banned in sport by WADA, and unscheduled but not approved by the FDA in the United States. [2]

Forum threads on looksmax.org present bromantane as a dopamine-supporting compound that increases motivation, lowers anxiety, and may help users on stimulant medication, citing Wikipedia and Russian literature. [7][8] Users trade impressions of effect from oral and other routes; some report little effect. [7]

Published human data consist mainly of Russian-language studies in asthenia and neurasthenia, including a 728-patient multicentre study, and military and sports-medicine reports. [2][6] No studies found in healthy people for appearance, hormonal or looksmaxxing-related outcomes.

lore.intro: Bromantane is discussed on looksmax.org as a dopamine-boosting nootropic for drive and stress, often alongside other recovery and mood compounds. [7][8]

claims.claim: Bromantane raises baseline dopamine and motivation
claims.believers: Forum posters say it increases dopamine synthesis at the gene-expression level, leaving more brain dopamine and improving drive and focus. [7][8]
claims.experts: Animal studies report increased tyrosine hydroxylase expression and altered dopamine metabolism; human evidence is limited to Russian asthenia studies. [2][4]

claims.claim: It lowers anxiety and social stress
claims.believers: Users describe a calmer, more confident mood and reduced chronic stress. [8]
claims.experts: Russian sources describe anxiolytic properties in neurasthenia patients; independent trials in healthy people are not published. [2]

claims.claim: It boosts testosterone and lowers prolactin, aiding physique
claims.believers: A looksmax.org overview argues indirect testosterone increases and prolactin reduction may improve muscle and physical appearance. [8]
claims.experts: No published human trial in healthy men was identified that measured testosterone or prolactin response to bromantane. [2]

claims.claim: It resensitises users to stimulants such as caffeine or methylphenidate
claims.believers: One poster reports that a small dose of methylphenidate felt much stronger after bromantane use. [8]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this interaction.

claims.claim: It is non-addictive and has minimal side effects
claims.believers: Posters cite the Russian literature describing no tolerance or withdrawal. [7]
claims.experts: Russian and animal studies report low toxicity and no dependence, while long-term data in healthy users are lacking and WADA bans the drug. [2]

card.summary: Russian adamantane stimulant-anxiolytic traded as a motivation nootropic; human data are small and mostly Russian-language.
card.note: Banned in sport by WADA; not FDA-approved; no appearance trials.

quick.overview:
Bromantane is a Russian-developed drug, sold there as Ladasten for neurasthenia (fatigue). It is described as a mild stimulant with anxiety-reducing effects.

In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed for motivation, stress and recovery, not as a direct appearance treatment. Most human evidence comes from Russian-language studies, and no trials address appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Animal research reports that it increases the enzymes that make dopamine (tyrosine hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase) instead of mainly blocking dopamine reuptake. The precise mechanism is not settled.
quick.risks: Russian studies report few side effects (about 3% of patients in one large study). Long-term data in healthy users are lacking. It is prescription-only in Russia, unapproved by the FDA, and banned by WADA since 1997.
